strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: selecting useful prior robot data for task-specific imitation learning rather than assuming that all additional data helps.

DataMIL provides a coherent model-aware alternative to similarity-based retrieval, combining datamodel influence estimates with a differentiable behavior-cloning proxy that avoids real-world rollouts during selection.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering all 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO tasks with Octo, and four real-world settings using heterogeneous Open X-Embodiment data, including cross-embodiment and multitask transfer.
Comparisons include several relevant retrieval methods (BehaviorRetrieval, FlowRetrieval, STRAP, and state/action heuristics), as well as target-only, all-data, or size-matched random controls.
The qualitative analyses of selected sources and expert versus suboptimal demonstrations help explain what the method is learning beyond aggregate success rates.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully support the paper's claims of consistent superiority. On LIBERO, DataMIL has the best average by only 1.36 percentage points over BehaviorRetrieval and is not the best method on most individual tasks; the reported per-task variability is much larger than this average gap, with no statistical significance analysis.

The real-world evaluation is underpowered: it uses a single training seed and only 10–39 rollouts per task, reports no confidence intervals, and DataMIL does not win Franka-Ball. The strong real-world and cross-embodiment conclusions therefore remain tentative.

The central proxy assumption is validated against rollout-based datamodeling on only one MetaWorld task. There is no systematic analysis of proxy-versus-success correlation across tasks, datasets, checkpoints, or policy classes, even though behavior-cloning loss can correlate poorly with closed-loop success under covariate shift.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the main technical contribution. Important details are missing, including the number of regression subset trainings, regression regularization, complete metagradient algorithm and truncation settings, optimization hyperparameters, compute requirements, and absolute runtime. The claim of an 8x speedup appears only as an isolated statement.

Several consequential design choices lack ablations: cluster granularity, selection fraction, co-training ratio, target-data split, number of target demonstrations, and the hand-designed pre-grasp weighting used only for LIBERO. It is unclear how sensitive the gains are to these choices or whether they were tuned on the reported tasks.

The novelty is moderate: the regression and metagradient estimators are adopted from prior datamodel/data-attribution work, while the principal robotics adaptation is to optimize held-out behavior-cloning loss and aggregate examples into temporal clusters. Stronger validation is needed to establish this proxy as a generally reliable contribution.

The MetaWorld setup contains expert demonstrations from every target task in the prior corpus, making much of the benefit attributable to recovering same-task expert data. Conversely, Octo is initialized from a checkpoint already pretrained on the OXE datasets being selected, so the OXE experiments are more accurately interpreted as task-specific reweighting or repeated exposure than clean selection from unseen prior data.

The method remains several times more expensive than ordinary training, yet there is no compute-matched comparison or detailed cost-benefit analysis. This weakens the practical case relative to inexpensive retrieval baselines.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: selecting useful prior demonstrations for task-specific robot imitation learning rather than indiscriminately co-training on heterogeneous data.

Adapting datamodel-based attribution to robotics through a differentiable behavior-cloning validation objective is intuitive and potentially useful, particularly because it avoids real-world rollouts during selection.
The empirical scope is commendably broad, covering 50 MetaWorld tasks, LIBERO-10 with Octo, and several real-robot tasks using subsets of Open X-Embodiment.

The comparison includes multiple relevant retrieval approaches, target-only training, and uncurated or random-data controls. The qualitative analysis of selected datasets also provides some insight into what the method retrieves.
weaknesses: The central surrogate assumption is inadequately validated. The paper argues that held-out behavior-cloning loss can replace rollout success based principally on one MetaWorld task and final selected-policy performance. It does not report correlations, ranking accuracy, or subset-level predictive performance across tasks, policy classes, or the distribution shifts where this assumption matters most.

The LIBERO improvement is weak: DataMIL averages 37.76% versus 36.4% for BR, with large per-task standard deviations and DataMIL losing to other methods on many individual tasks. No paired significance analysis or aggregate uncertainty is reported, so the claimed consistent advantage is unsupported.

The real-world evidence is too small and noisy for the strength of the conclusions. Evaluation uses only 14–39 rollouts per setting and a single random seed, reports no confidence intervals, and sometimes awards half credit for partial completion. This cannot establish reliable superiority, especially for a high-variance robotics pipeline.

Several evaluation inconsistencies reduce confidence. The OXE text says All-Data is replaced by a size-matched Random baseline, whereas Table 3 labels the corresponding column All-Data. The same task is variously called Franka-Pick and Franka-Ball. These ambiguities make it difficult to determine exactly what was compared.

Important ablations are missing: selection budget, target-set size, number of datamodel-training steps or subsets, clustering scale, target-data mixing, pre-grasp weighting, and sensitivity to seeds. There is also no direct comparison of datamodel quality or compute-quality tradeoffs between regression and metagradient estimators beyond a single illustrative example.

Baseline and hyperparameter selection may not be adequately controlled. DataMIL uses manually chosen pre-grasp up-weighting in LIBERO, task-dependent OXE selection ratios, and dataset-specific clustering choices described as having been found effective, but the validation protocol is unspecified. Comparable tuning opportunities or privileged information are not demonstrated for the baselines.

The technical novelty is moderate: the core attribution estimators are taken from prior work, while the robotics-specific additions—validation behavior-cloning loss, temporal clustering, and mixing target data—are relatively straightforward. Moreover, the first-order linear approximation is used to select subsets far from its expansion point without theoretical justification or broad empirical fidelity tests.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the core method. Essential estimator settings, computational cost, training hyperparameters, and automated details of the pre-grasp labeling are missing; the real-world target datasets and evaluation setup are not provided. The reliance on very recent attribution methods does not substitute for a self-contained implementation description.

Overall, the idea is promising and the breadth is attractive, but the evidence does not robustly establish the main claims. The lack of surrogate validation, statistical support, controlled ablations, and reproducible methodological detail places the work below the acceptance threshold for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: Clear and practically important problem: selecting useful prior robot data for task-specific imitation learning without requiring costly environment rollouts.
DataMIL offers a coherent adaptation of datamodel-based attribution to robotics, combining a differentiable validation-loss proxy, temporal clustering, and efficient metagradient estimation.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering all 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO tasks with an Octo policy, and several real-world tasks using heterogeneous Open X-Embodiment data.
Comparisons include multiple relevant retrieval heuristics, target-only, all-data or size-matched random controls, and generally use matched selection budgets and downstream training procedures.

Results provide meaningful positive evidence: DataMIL clearly improves average MetaWorld performance, narrowly leads on LIBERO, and obtains particularly large gains in the challenging real-world experiments.
The qualitative analyses of selected datasets, embodiments, and high- versus low-ranked examples help explain behavior beyond aggregate success rates.
The presentation is clear, well organized, and candid about computational cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, and limited target-task scale.
weaknesses: The central surrogate assumption is under-validated. Agreement between held-out behavior-cloning loss and rollout success is studied primarily through one MetaWorld task and final performance, without quantitative correlation, ranking fidelity, or extensive counterexamples across LIBERO and real-world settings.

Several important design choices lack ablations, including cluster granularity, selection fraction, target-data split, target-data amount, co-training ratio, and the LIBERO-specific pre-grasp weighting. This makes it difficult to separate the core datamodel contribution from task-dependent tuning.

Real-world evidence is promising but statistically limited: each policy uses a single training seed, only 14–39 total evaluations per setting, no confidence intervals or significance tests, and partially subjective half-credit outcomes in the multitask setting.

The LIBERO advantage is modest—37.76% versus 36.4% for Behavior Retrieval—and DataMIL is not consistently best task by task. Uncertainty estimates overlap substantially, so the claim of consistent superiority is stronger than the evidence supports.

Scalability and reproducibility are not documented sufficiently. The paper omits concrete estimator costs, number of optimization runs or metagradient steps, memory requirements, wall-clock comparisons beyond a single 8x statement, and enough implementation detail to reproduce the metagradient pipeline.

Novelty is more integrative than fundamental: the datamodel estimators are adopted from prior work, while the principal robotics additions—validation-loss proxying, clustering, and mixing target data—are sensible but technically incremental.

The formulation describes model-aware selection as directly optimizing task success, but the scalable experiments actually optimize behavior-cloning loss; the relationship between these objectives can fail under covariate shift and multimodal demonstrations and deserves a more qualified treatment.

Using an Octo checkpoint already pretrained on the OXE sources complicates interpretation of the OXE selection results: the experiment measures selection during further adaptation from data already represented in the initialization, rather than clean transfer from an unseen prior corpus.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: selecting useful data from large, heterogeneous robot datasets for task-specific imitation learning.

DataMIL provides a coherent policy-aware alternative to hand-designed similarity heuristics, combining datamodel-based attribution with an offline behavior-cloning-loss proxy that avoids real-world rollouts during selection.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering all 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO tasks with an Octo policy, and four real-robot settings using subsets of Open X-Embodiment data. The cross-embodiment Tiago experiment and multitask DROID setting are particularly valuable.

The paper compares against several relevant retrieval methods under a largely unified downstream training protocol and includes useful ablations of selection fraction, temporal cluster size, co-training ratio, proxy versus rollout objectives, and All-Data training duration.

Qualitative analyses of selected data and the transparent discussion of computational cost help explain the method's behavior and practical tradeoffs. The paper is generally clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: The strongest controlled result is MetaWorld, but its prior dataset contains scripted expert demonstrations for the exact target tasks. Much of the gain can therefore arise from identifying those demonstrations and filtering suboptimal trajectories, making this setting less convincing as evidence of transfer from genuinely different prior tasks.

The LIBERO advantage is weak: DataMIL averages 37.76% versus 36.40% for BR, and it is not the best method on most individual tasks. No uncertainty or significance analysis is reported for the aggregate comparison, so the claim of consistent superiority is stronger than the evidence.

Several LIBERO hyperparameters, including pre-grasp weighting, cluster size, selection ratio, and co-training ratio, are chosen using LIBERO-5, whose five tasks are included in the reported LIBERO-10 evaluation. This creates test-task tuning and is especially consequential given the small final margin over baselines.

The real-robot results use only one training seed and very few evaluations—14, 17, 39, or roughly 10 per multitask component. Consequently, differences often correspond to only a few successful rollouts and lack confidence intervals. DataMIL also does not win every individual setting, despite language suggesting consistent gains.

The OXE baseline description is inconsistent: the text says All-Data is replaced by a size-matched Random baseline, while Table 1 labels the corresponding column All-Data. This ambiguity prevents a clear interpretation of an important comparison.

The metagradient algorithm is insufficiently specified and appears internally inconsistent. Counts are declared binary and initialized to one, yet the update c <- c - sign(g)·m can move them outside {0,1}; moreover, because M is defined as a metric to maximize and later instantiated as negative loss, subtracting a positive gradient appears to remove beneficial data. The relationship among the stored masked gradients, iterative count updates, and final ranking also needs a precise derivation.

The proxy-versus-rollout validation covers only four MetaWorld tasks, while the central scalability claims rely on the proxy with a different diffusion policy and substantially more heterogeneous LIBERO/OXE data. Direct correlation, ranking-quality, or held-out subset-prediction measurements in those regimes are missing.

DataMIL remains expensive—up to 3–4 days on four A100 GPUs for OXE and several times the cost of ordinary policy training—and requires task-specific attribution runs. The paper does not compare performance at matched total compute or establish when this overhead is preferable to additional fine-tuning or simpler model-aware alternatives.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript refers to a project website without providing an accessible link, and important implementation details for the specialized metagradient machinery are delegated to recent external work. Exact data splits, seeds, and statistical evaluation procedures are not fully documented.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important practical problem: selecting useful prior robot data based on downstream policy behavior rather than hand-designed similarity alone.
The offline proxy objective, temporal clustering, and target-data mixing form a sensible adaptation of datamodels to imitation learning.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO tasks, and several real-robot OXE settings. The real-world average improvement is promising.

The paper is generally clear and includes useful ablations, task-level results, qualitative analyses, and an honest accounting of computational cost. weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. The two estimators are taken from prior work, while the main adaptations—held-out behavior-cloning loss, clustering, and mixing target data—are relatively straightforward. The paper lacks comparisons to simpler gradient-influence or data-reweighting alternatives that could establish the necessity of the full method.

The central surrogate-metric claim is weakly validated. Only four MetaWorld tasks compare proxy-based selection with rollout-based selection, and the paper reports final performance of one selected subset rather than correlation, ranking accuracy, or held-out predictive quality of the datamodel. No analogous validation is provided for the substantially different diffusion-policy settings in LIBERO or OXE.

The LIBERO gain is not convincing: DataMIL averages 37.76 versus 36.40 for BR, with large per-task variability, no significance analysis, and DataMIL failing to be the best method on most individual tasks. This does not support claims of consistent superiority.

LIBERO-5, comprising five tasks from the reported LIBERO-10 evaluation suite, is used to choose the selection fraction, cluster size, and co-training ratio. The pre-grasp weighting was also adopted after observing improved LIBERO performance. This amounts to tuning on a substantial portion of the test benchmark and is especially concerning given the small final margin.

The real-robot results use only one training seed and merely 10–39 evaluation trials per task, with no confidence intervals. At these sample sizes, one rollout changes some reported scores by 7–10 percentage points. Task-specific selection ratios and the inclusion of half-credit partial successes further complicate interpretation.

The estimator description has reproducibility and consistency problems. Algorithm 2 declares binary counts but its update can produce negative values or values above one, and it returns a collection of masked gradients rather than a clearly defined final attribution vector. The claim of exact metagradients is also qualified later by differentiation through only the last 100 training steps. The main-text regression equation contains inconsistent indices, while regularization, intercept handling, and several stochastic details are unspecified.

DataMIL is extremely expensive: the OXE estimator requires 3–4 days on four A100 GPUs for a target setting and is reported as 3–5 times slower than ordinary policy training. This substantially weakens the claimed practicality and scalability of data selection.

Overall, the breadth and promising real-world trends are valuable, but the incremental method, test-set tuning, weak statistical evidence, insufficient surrogate validation, and underspecified estimator prevent the work from meeting the evidentiary standard of a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem in robot learning and offers a compelling model-aware alternative to similarity-based data retrieval. Using an offline differentiable proxy makes datamodel-based selection applicable without costly or unsafe real-world rollouts. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/2029354de5a94ce29f103d30412c799b/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical scope is strong: experiments cover all 50 MetaWorld tasks, LIBERO-10 with an Octo policy, and several real-robot tasks using heterogeneous OXE data, including cross-embodiment and multitask settings.
The real-world results are promising. DataMIL obtains a 61.0 average versus 40.0 for the strongest reported baseline, with especially large gains on Franka-Pouch and Tiago-Sink.

The evaluation includes relevant retrieval baselines, target-only and all-data/random controls, task-level results, qualitative analysis, and ablations of selection percentage, cluster size, co-training ratio, and longer all-data training.
The appendices provide substantial implementation, dataset, hyperparameter, and computational-cost information, and the paper candidly discusses scalability and hyperparameter limitations.
weaknesses: The LIBERO advantage is modest: the average is 37.76 versus 36.40 for BR, and DataMIL is the best method on only two of ten individual tasks. Reported uncertainties often overlap, but no paired statistical tests or confidence intervals for aggregate improvements are provided. Claims of consistent superiority are therefore overstated.

Real-robot evidence is based on a single training seed and only 10–39 evaluations per setting, without uncertainty estimates. Fixed object configurations and partial-success scoring in Droid further limit confidence in robustness and statistical significance.

The central proxy-metric claim lacks direct validation through held-out-subset prediction correlations, rank correlations, or calibration. Comparing policies trained from selected data on four MetaWorld tasks is useful but does not establish that the proxy reliably approximates rollout performance across datasets and policy classes.

The metagradient presentation contains reproducibility-relevant ambiguities: Algorithm 2 subtracts sign(g) even though M is formulated as a maximization metric, its update can move counts outside the stated binary domain, and the relationship between the claimed exact influence computation and differentiation through only the final k training steps is insufficiently explained.

Hyperparameters are ablated on LIBERO-5, which is itself a subset of the reported LIBERO-10 evaluation tasks, raising a tuning-on-test concern. The LIBERO-specific pre-grasp weighting also introduces hand-designed prior knowledge whose contribution is not isolated.

Octo is initialized from a checkpoint previously trained on the same OXE sources subsequently used for selection. Although shared across methods, this complicates interpreting the experiments as clean evidence about selecting genuinely new prior data.

The method remains expensive—3–5 times standard training and several days on four A100 GPUs for OXE—and selection ratios and clustering granularity remain task-dependent. The conceptual novelty is primarily an adaptation of existing datamodel and metagradient machinery rather than a fundamentally new estimator.
